name: Know-your-customer onboarding of a new corporate client at a commercial bank
function: client onboarding and financial crimes compliance
summary: This process takes one new corporate client of a US commercial bank from the relationship manager's onboarding request to open accounts, or to a decline or abandonment. Onboarding staff collect formation documents, the beneficial ownership certification and a KYC questionnaire; KYC analysts verify the entity and its owners, write the customer profile, screen every related name for sanctions, politically exposed persons and negative news, and rate the client's risk. High-risk clients go through enhanced due diligence and senior compliance and business approval before deposit operations open the accounts. Most of the elapsed time is spent waiting for the client to supply missing documents, with several chase rounds, and in queues between the onboarding, compliance and operations teams, while data is re-keyed between CRM, KYC and core systems.

baseline.org_archetype: A US regional commercial bank with about 8,000 employees that banks small and mid-size companies through relationship managers, with a central client onboarding team, a financial crimes compliance unit and deposit operations.
baseline.notes: Covers legal entity clients onboarded by relationship managers (operating accounts and treasury services), not small businesses opening a single account in a branch, and not credit approval.

unit_of_work: one new corporate (legal entity) client relationship
trigger: A relationship manager submits an onboarding request for a company that has agreed to bank with the bank.
end_state: The client's accounts and services are open and the KYC file is approved and stored, or the relationship is declined, or the client abandons onboarding.

volume.seasonality: Higher in the first and fourth quarters as RMs close annual targets; dips in summer.

evidence.note: Author estimate for a regional commercial bank; FinCEN's 2016 estimate of about 8 million new legal entity accounts a year across all US covered institutions gives the national scale.

triggered_by.from: Commercial lending (new borrower needing deposit accounts)

produces.object: open accounts and online banking credentials

produces.to: Transaction monitoring and periodic KYC review
produces.object: customer risk rating and expected activity profile

produces.to: OFAC and FinCEN (when a sanctions match or suspicious activity is found)
produces.object: blocking or rejection report, suspicious activity report

systems.name: KYC / client lifecycle management workflow with risk rating model
Document repository and secure client upload portal
Secretary of State business registries, commercial identity and company data services
Sanctions, PEP and adverse media screening tool with alert case management
Core deposit system, online banking and treasury services set-up

steps.name: Submit onboarding request
steps.description: After agreeing to bank a new corporate client, the relationship manager opens an onboarding request in the CRM with the legal name, entity type, products wanted (operating accounts, treasury services, credit), expected balances and activity, and client contacts. The RM often adds notes from the sales calls.

error.defect_description: Expected activity, entity type or owners described vaguely or wrongly.

evidence.note: RM-initiated onboarding is standard in commercial banking; minutes and the error rate are author estimates.

steps.name: Create KYC case and re-key client data
steps.description: An onboarding specialist picks up the request, creates a case in the KYC workflow tool and re-types the entity name, address, tax ID, products and contacts from the CRM because the two systems are not linked. The specialist checks for an existing relationship or a prior declined case.

error.defect_description: Typo in legal name or tax ID carried into screening and account set-up.

evidence.note: GLEIF reports institutions use on average four internal identifiers and about a quarter of onboarding is manual; minutes and queue time are author estimates.

steps.name: Send document checklist and KYC questionnaire
steps.description: The specialist selects the checklist for the entity type (corporation, LLC, partnership, nonprofit) and emails it with the KYC questionnaire and beneficial ownership certification form to the client contact, copying the RM.

error.defect_description: Wrong checklist for the entity type, causing a second request.

evidence.note: Document set follows the CIP and beneficial ownership rules; minutes are author estimates.

steps.name: Client gathers and returns documents
steps.description: The client's finance or legal staff collect articles of incorporation or organisation, operating or partnership agreement, IRS tax ID letter or W-9, certificate of good standing, signed beneficial ownership certification, IDs for owners and signers, board resolution and the completed questionnaire, and upload or email them.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Surveys report banks ask for many documents with no common standard; the 1 to 21 day wait (mode 5) is an author estimate.

steps.name: Check documents for completeness
steps.description: The specialist opens each document, ticks it off the checklist, checks signatures, dates and that names match across documents, and confirms every 25% owner and a control person appear on the certification. Gaps are listed for the client.
outputs: complete file or list of gaps

error.defect_description: A missing or expired document is not noticed.

control.basis: Beneficial ownership rule, 31 CFR 1010.230: identify 25% owners and one control person at account opening

evidence.note: Banks report contacting clients about 4 times per onboarding and corporates about 8 times; 15% of banks contact clients ten or more times. The 50% gap rate at each completeness check is an author estimate consistent with these counts.

steps.name: Chase client for missing items
steps.description: The specialist emails the client a list of the missing or defective items and, when replies stall, asks the RM to call the client. Each chase is logged in the case.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Repeated client contacts are reported by both surveys; minutes are author estimates.

steps.name: Client sends missing items
steps.description: The client finds the missing pages, signs the certification, obtains a current good standing certificate or explains the ownership structure, and sends them. Some clients lose patience and stop responding.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

next.condition: client stops responding or goes elsewhere

evidence.note: 12% of corporates reported changing banks because of KYC issues; the per-chase drop-out and waits are author estimates.

steps.name: Verify legal entity existence and identity
steps.description: A KYC analyst checks the entity on the state business registry (status, formation date, registered agent, officers), matches the tax ID and address, compares formation documents with the registry record, and records the evidence in the case.

error.defect_description: Registry mismatch (name change, dissolved status) missed.

control.basis: Customer Identification Program, 31 CFR 1020.220: verify a non-individual customer's existence through documents or non-documentary methods

evidence.note: Verification methods from the CIP rule; minutes and queue are author estimates.

steps.name: Identify and verify beneficial owners and control person
steps.description: The analyst builds an ownership chart from the certification and agreements, traces owners through holding companies, and verifies each 25% owner and the control person against identity databases or ID copies. Layered or foreign ownership often needs more documents from the client.

error.defect_description: An indirect owner above 25% missed in a layered structure.

control.basis: Beneficial ownership rule, 31 CFR 1010.230(b)(2): verify identity of each beneficial owner using risk-based procedures including CIP elements

next.condition: ownership unclear or verification fails: more documents needed

evidence.note: FinCEN estimated 20 to 40 minutes per legal entity customer to identify, verify, review and record beneficial owners; the 12% return rate is an author estimate.

steps.name: Document nature, purpose and expected activity
steps.description: The analyst writes the customer profile: business description and industry code, countries of operation, sources of revenue, products, expected monthly deposits, wires, cash and international payments, and the reason for the relationship. Vague RM notes are clarified by email.

error.defect_description: Expected activity understated, which later drives monitoring false alerts or a missed risk factor.

control.basis: AML program rule, 31 CFR 1020.210(a)(2)(v): understand the nature and purpose of customer relationships to develop a customer risk profile

evidence.note: Requirement stated in the rule; minutes are author estimates.

steps.name: Screen names against sanctions, PEP and adverse media lists
steps.description: The screening tool checks the entity, its trade names, owners, control person, signers and directors against OFAC and other sanctions lists, politically exposed person lists and negative news. Possible matches open alerts for review.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

control.basis: OFAC sanctions regulations (31 CFR chapter V) and CIP comparison with government lists, 31 CFR 1020.220(a)(4)

evidence.note: Screening is required; the 35% chance that at least one of five to eight names produces an alert is an author estimate based on common fuzzy-matching settings.

steps.name: Review screening alerts
steps.description: A screening analyst compares each alert with the client data (date of birth, nationality, address, ownership) and the list entry, discounts false positives with a written rationale, and escalates possible true matches, confirmed PEPs or relevant negative news.

error.defect_description: A true match is discounted as a false positive.

control.basis: OFAC sanctions compliance: no dealings with blocked persons; documented alert disposition

next.condition: possible true match, PEP or relevant adverse media

evidence.note: Alert review practice is standard; the 12% escalation rate and minutes are author estimates (most name-screening alerts are false positives).

steps.name: Investigate escalated match
steps.description: An investigator researches the escalated name in depth, confirms or rules out the sanctions match, assesses the PEP's role and the news, and records the conclusion. A confirmed sanctions match stops onboarding and triggers blocking or rejection reporting.

error.defect_description: Relevant adverse news judged immaterial.

control.basis: OFAC regulations: reject or block and report within 10 business days (31 CFR 501.603/501.604)

next.condition: cleared or confirmed PEP/adverse media for risk rating
confirmed sanctions match or unacceptable risk

evidence.note: Reporting duty from the OFAC regulation; minutes, queue and shares are author estimates.

steps.name: Assign customer risk rating
steps.description: The analyst runs the risk rating model in the KYC tool, which scores industry, geography, products, ownership complexity, PEP status, cash intensity and screening results, checks the result against the profile and documents any override.

error.defect_description: Risk understated, so enhanced due diligence is skipped.

control.basis: AML program rule, 31 CFR 1020.210(a)(2)(v): customer risk profile; bank's board-approved risk rating methodology

evidence.note: Risk profile is required by rule; the model and the 12% high-risk share are author estimates for a regional commercial book.

steps.name: Request enhanced due diligence information
steps.description: The relationship manager asks the client for source of funds and wealth, details of international payments and counterparties, cash handling, licences (for example money services or cannabis-adjacent businesses) and, for some clients, arranges a site visit.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: EDD information types are standard bank practice; FFIEC manual guidance not opened; minutes and waits are author estimates.

steps.name: Quality check the KYC file
steps.description: A QC reviewer re-checks the file before approval: every required document present and current, entity and owner verification evidenced, screening alerts dispositioned, profile and risk rating supported. Failures go back to the analyst or, for missing evidence, to the client.

error.defect_description: A gap passes QC.

control.basis: Four-eyes review of KYC files under the bank's BSA/AML program; supports independent testing and examination findings

next.condition: analyst rework of profile, rating or evidence

evidence.note: Pre-approval QC is common practice; pass rate, minutes and queue are author estimates.

steps.name: Perform enhanced due diligence review
steps.description: An EDD investigator reviews the client's EDD answers and documents, researches owners and counterparties in depth, compares expected activity with the business model, and writes an EDD memo with a recommendation and any account restrictions or monitoring conditions.

error.defect_description: Source of funds accepted without adequate support.

control.basis: Risk-based customer due diligence for higher-risk customers under 31 CFR 1020.210(a)(2)(v) and bank BSA/AML policy

next.condition: more information needed from the client

evidence.note: EDD depth beyond the CDD rule is set by bank policy; minutes and queue are author estimates.

steps.name: Client provides enhanced due diligence information
steps.description: The client prepares explanations and documents on ownership history, source of funds, major customers and suppliers, and international activity, and may host a site visit.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

evidence.note: Client response time and refusal share are author estimates.

steps.name: Approve high-risk client (compliance)
steps.description: The BSA/AML officer or a delegated compliance manager reads the EDD memo and QC notes and approves, approves with conditions such as transaction limits or more frequent reviews, sends back for more information, or declines.

error.defect_description: Approval without addressing a memo gap.

control.basis: Bank BSA/AML policy: senior compliance approval to onboard high-risk customers

evidence.note: Senior approval for high-risk customers is common policy; FFIEC manual guidance not opened; times and shares are author estimates.

steps.name: Business executive sign-off for high-risk client
steps.description: The commercial market executive reviews the relationship's value against the compliance conditions and signs off on accepting the risk, or decides not to proceed.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

control.basis: Bank risk acceptance policy: line-of-business ownership of high-risk relationships

evidence.note: Dual compliance and business sign-off is common but not universal; author estimate.

steps.name: Open accounts and set up signers and services
steps.description: A deposit operations specialist creates the customer and accounts in the core system, re-keying data from the KYC case, adds authorised signers, sets up online banking users and entitlements and treasury services such as ACH and wires, and records the risk rating and review date.

error.defect_description: Wrong signer, entitlement, product code or tax ID keyed.

control.basis: CIP, 31 CFR 1020.220: account opened only after required identifying information is obtained; KYC approval recorded before opening

evidence.note: Re-keying between the KYC tool and the core was common in 2019-2022; minutes and error rate are author estimates.

steps.name: Decline relationship and record decision
steps.description: The KYC analyst records the decline reason, notifies the RM, who tells the client the bank cannot proceed, and flags the entity and owners in the KYC tool. For a confirmed sanctions match, compliance files the rejection or blocking report and considers a suspicious activity report.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

control.basis: OFAC reporting of blocked or rejected transactions (31 CFR 501.603-604) and record retention under 31 CFR 1010.230(i)

evidence.note: Reporting and retention duties from the cited rules; minutes are author estimates.

steps.name: Close abandoned onboarding case
steps.description: After the client stops responding past the follow-up limit, the onboarding specialist confirms with the RM, closes the case as withdrawn and keeps the collected documents and verification records.

error.defect_description: None introduced.

control.basis: Record retention for identification and verification records, 31 CFR 1010.230(i) and 1020.220(a)(3)

evidence.note: Surveys report client abandonment during onboarding; the follow-up limit (about 10 to 21 days) is an author estimate.

steps.name: Check account set-up against approved file
steps.description: A second deposit operations specialist compares the core set-up with the approved KYC file and signed agreements, field by field for names, tax ID, signers, limits and entitlements, and returns errors for correction.

error.defect_description: Set-up error passes the check.

control.basis: Maker-checker control on account and entitlement set-up

evidence.note: Maker-checker on set-up is common practice; author estimate.

steps.name: Release accounts and send welcome package
steps.description: The onboarding specialist confirms the accounts are active, sends the client the account numbers, online banking credentials and treasury service instructions, notifies the RM and closes the case.

error.defect_description: Credentials sent to the wrong contact.

evidence.note: Author estimate.

exceptions.name: Incomplete documents
exceptions.description: The first package lacks a signed certification, a current good standing certificate, owner IDs or an agreement, so the specialist chases the client, often more than once.

exceptions.name: Layered or unclear ownership
exceptions.description: Owners sit behind holding companies, trusts or foreign entities and the analyst needs more documents to trace 25% owners.

exceptions.name: Screening escalation
exceptions.description: An alert looks like a true sanctions match, a PEP or relevant negative news and goes to an investigator; a confirmed sanctions match ends in a decline and report.

exceptions.name: High-risk client
exceptions.description: The risk rating is high (industry, geography, cash intensity, PEP) and the client goes through enhanced due diligence and two senior approvals.

exceptions.name: QC failure
exceptions.description: QC finds unsupported profile entries, missing verification evidence or undispositioned alerts and returns the file.

exceptions.name: Account set-up error
exceptions.description: The checker finds a wrong signer, entitlement or tax ID in the core set-up.

exceptions.name: Client abandons
exceptions.description: The client stops responding during document collection or EDD and the case is closed.

benchmarks.population: Corporate client onboarding at banks, 2017-2019 surveys

evidence.note: Thomson Reuters 2017: average 26 days reported by banks and 32 days by corporates; GLEIF 2018: typically 6 weeks, 43% within a month and 26% over two months. The p50 and p90 are read from these, not measured medians.
Stated in the survey write-up.

evidence.note: Estimated time to identify, verify, review and record beneficial ownership per legal entity customer.
Stated in the survey write-up.

evidence.note: Stated in the survey results.

pain_points.description: Clients are asked for documents several times because checklists differ by bank and first packages are often incomplete, which is the largest source of delay and of client frustration.

evidence.note: Corporates report about 8 contacts per onboarding; 15% of banks contact clients ten or more times.

pain_points.description: Client and entity data is typed into the CRM, re-keyed into the KYC tool and keyed again into the core system, creating errors that QC and the set-up checker must catch.

evidence.note: GLEIF found institutions use about four internal identifiers per client and a quarter of onboarding is manual.

pain_points.description: Most screening alerts are false positives, yet each needs a documented review, and escalations queue for scarce investigators.

evidence.note: Widely reported in the industry; no source opened gives a rate.

pain_points.description: High-risk clients wait days in the EDD queue and again for two senior approvers, adding two to four weeks.

evidence.note: Author estimate from the step waits.

assumptions: External steps (client actions) carry zero touch time; the client's effort is inside the waits, so the staffing comparison reflects bank labour only.
The 50% incomplete rate at each completeness check (about 1.9 document rounds per case) are set to match the survey finding of about four bank contacts (eight as clients count them) per onboarding.
Screening alert, escalation and high-risk shares (35%, 12% of alerted cases, 12% of cases) are author estimates; no source with these rates was opened.

Senior compliance and business approval for high-risk clients and pre-approval QC follow common US practice; the FFIEC BSA/AML manual was not reachable, so these controls are marked as bank policy rather than law.

Cycle-time benchmarks come from 2017-2019 global surveys that mix commercial, corporate and investment banking clients; a US regional commercial bank's middle-market clients are likely nearer the lower end.
Credit approval for clients that also borrow runs in a separate process and is not included; treasury services implementation after account opening is a separate downstream process.
Stated FTEs are about 15% above the hands-on time implied at 130 productive hours a month, to cover case administration, rework not modelled and periodic reviews handled by the same teams.
Loaded cost = BLS May 2021 hourly wage x 1.49 (benefits: wages are 67% of compensation in financial activities, BLS ECEC Dec 2021) x 1.2 for overhead (author estimate), about 1.8 x wage.
